metadata.title: Agentic AI: The age of reasoning—A review
metadata.abstract_summary: This paper provides a comprehensive review of agentic AI, focusing on its evolution and three core aspects: patterns, types, and environments. The evolution of agentic AI is traced through five phases to the current era of multi-modal and collaborative agents, driven by advancements in reinforcement learning, neural networks, and large language models (LLMs).

sections.heading: Pozi
sections.text: a , ∗ a School of Computing, Universiti Utara Malaysia (UUM), Sintok, 06010, Kedah, Malaysia b The Mediterranean and Gulf Cooperative Insurance and Reinsurance Company (MEDGULF), Riyadh, 12622, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Agentic AI Autonomous systems Artificial intelligence Large language models (LLMs) Reasoning agents AI taxonomy A B S T R A C T Artificial intelligence has experienced a significant boom with the emergence of agentic AI, where autonomous agents are increasingly replacing human intervention, enabling systems to perceive, reason, and act indepen- dently to achieve specific goals. Despite its transformative potential, comprehensive information on agentic AI remains scarce in the literature. This paper provides the first comprehensive review of agentic AI, focusing on its evolution and three core aspects: patterns, types, and environments. The evolution of agentic AI is traced through five phases to the current era of multi-modal and collaborative agents, driven by advancements in reinforcement learning, neural networks, and large language models (LLMs). Five key patterns: tool use, reflection, ReAct, planning, and multi-agent collaboration (MAC) define how agentic AI systems interact and process tasks. These systems are categorized into seven categories, each tailored for specific operational styles and autonomy in decision making. The environments in which these agents operate are classified as static, dynamic, fully observable, partially observable, deterministic, stochastic, single-agent, and multi- agent, emphasizing the impact of environmental complexity on agent behavior. Agentic AI has revolutionized systems through autonomous decision making and resource optimization, yet challenges persist in aligning AI with human values, ensuring adaptability, and addressing ethical constraints. Future research focuses on multidomain agents, human–AI collaboration, and self-improving systems. This work provides researchers, practitioners, and policymakers with a structured approach to understanding and advancing the rapidly evolving landscape of agentic AI systems. 1.

claims.text: Artificial intelligence has experienced a significant boom with the emergence of agentic AI, where autonomous agents are increasingly replacing human intervention, enabling systems to perceive, reason, and act independently to achieve specific goals.

The evolution of agentic AI is traced through five phases to the current era of multi-modal and collaborative agents, driven by advancements in reinforcement learning, neural networks, and large language models (LLMs).
This paper provides the first comprehensive review of agentic AI, focusing on its evolution and three core aspects: patterns, types, and environments.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: The advent of agentic AI marks a transformative era in the digital landscape, redefining the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in human life and industries. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has emphasized the exponential growth of AI agents, suggesting that ‘‘there could possibly be more AI agents in the world than humans’’. Echoing this sentiment, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang envisions a paradigm shift from tools to skills, stating: ‘‘Our industry has been an industry of tools, but for the very first time, this is going to be an industry of skills. You can say the agents’’. He further adds, ‘‘We are going to have agents that are excellent at particular skills’’. These perspectives illuminate the unprecedented potential of agentic AI to revolutionize industries, foster innovation, and seamlessly integrate into the fabric of daily life. Agentic AI is the AI systems/programs designed to act autonomously, mimicking human-like behaviors and decision-making processes. These systems are capable of perceiving their environment, reasoning, and taking actions to achieve specific goals, exhibiting a level of agency Peer review under responsibility of Chongqing University. ∗ Corresponding author. E-mail addresses: nisa_ume@ahsgs.uum.edu.my (U. Nisa), muhammadshirazi@hotmail.com (M. Shirazi), mdali@uum.edu.my (M.A. Saip), syafiq.pozi@uum.edu.my (M.S.M. Pozi). similar to that of human beings. Agentic AI systems are intelligent, autonomous systems that can independently make decisions, learn from data, and adapt to changing environments without relying on external support or intervention [ 1 ]. Agentic AI systems improve human action by autonomously han- dling complex, multitasking tasks, shifting AI from passive assistance to strategic problem solving. Unlike traditional AI confined to rigid parameters, these systems dynamically adapt to complex and dynamic evolving environments, pursuing long-term goals with minimal or no human intervention. Rather than merely executing predefined instruc- tions, it augments human capabilities by initiating actions and mak- ing contextually informed choices, fostering collaborative innovation. The age of reasoning in AI is a transformative phase in the evolution of AI systems, in which agents (AI systems) begin to mimic aspects of human cognition. sections.heading: Agentic
sections.text: AI evolution Agentic AI has gained momentum in recent years, but it is already reshaping the landscape of autonomous decision making, adaptive learning, and human-AI collaboration across various domains. The evolution of agentic AI has been driven by advancements in machine learning, reinforcement learning, multi-agent systems, and cognitive architectures. This paper presents a chronological overview of the field, highlighting key milestones, influential research papers, and tech- nological breakthroughs. Its foundations can be traced back to the very beginnings of AI research in the 1950s, when pioneers like Alan Turing [ 18 ] raised the question of whether machines could ‘think’ in 1950, and when the Dartmouth Workshop [ 19 ] formally defined ‘Artificial Intelligence’ as a field in 1956. However, the notion of agents specifically began to crystallize in the 1980s, with work on symbolic planning, expert systems, and especially robotic architectures such as Ref. [ 20 ] that emphasized embodied, goal-driven behavior. By organizing the evolution of agentic AI into distinct phases (see Fig. 2 ), we provide a structured narrative of its development and identify trends that will shape its future. 2.1. The early foundations (1980s–1990s) The concept of agentic AI emerged in the 1980s and 1990s, driven by foundational research in artificial intelligence, robotics, and cogni- tive science. The research published in Ref. [ 20 ] introduced behavior- based AI, emphasizing the importance of interaction with the envi- ronment over symbolic reasoning. This publication presents a layered control system that enables autonomous robots to operate with increas- ing competence. Its modular, hierarchical design allows for adaptive learning and goal-oriented decision-making. This work laid the ground- work for embodied and situated agents. In parallel, Aloimonos et al. [ 21 ] proposed active vision. The concept of Active vision reflects agentic AI principles, where intelligence emerges through interaction with the environment, and tasks such as navigation, manipulation, and learning are critical for the agent’s adaptability and goal-driven behavior. Shortly thereafter, Ref. [ 22 ] argued that intelligence could emerge from the interaction of simple behaviors rather than complex internal models, demonstrating a layered control system in which autonomous robots operate with increasing competence. It introduced a decentralized parallel architecture where independent activity produc- ers interface with the real world, enabling autonomous decision-making and adaptability, key traits of agentic AI. Concurrently, researchers explored more formal characterizations of rational agents. The concept of rational agents was introduced by Ref. [ 23 ]. These rational agents act as entities that perceive and act to achieve goals. In the same year, Ref. [ 24 ] established the foundations of multi-agent systems (MAS), en- abling collaborative and competitive agent interactions. sections.heading: Key
sections.text: aspects of agentic AI 3.1. Patterns of agentic AI Agentic AI patterns are design patterns or frameworks used to structure and implement agentic behavior in AI systems. These patterns explain how agentic AI systems interact, process tasks, and respond to user input. It focuses on structural methodologies for building systems (agents). The researchers [ 3 , 83 ] explored four basic patterns of agentic AI frameworks: tool use, allowing external resource integration; reflec- tion, fostering iterative self-correction; planning, supporting structured task decomposition; and multi-agent collaboration (MAC), coordinat- ing multiple LMs for specialized sub-tasks. Table 3 comprehensively describes the different patterns of agentic AI. 3.2. A taxonomic framework to classify agentic AI Based on our systematic review, this study proposes a progressive taxonomic framework to classify agentic AI systems. Fig. 3 provides a hierarchical taxonomy of Agentic AI types, underscoring the grad- ual advancement in autonomy, adaptability, and cognitive complexity from reactive agents to self-aware systems. The following are agen- tic AI categorized into several distinct types based on capabilities, decision-making autonomy, and learning mechanisms. 3.2.1. Reactive agents Reactive agents are based on current input without memory or previous experiences [ 84 ]. These agents follow predefined rules or heuristics and cannot adapt their behavior dynamically. They are ef- ficient for well-defined tasks, but lack learning capabilities. Brooks [ 20 ] and Matarić [ 85 ] emphasized simplicity through modular designs, where complex behaviors are decomposed into simpler, independent modules. This modularity not only facilitates rapid response to changes in the environment but also simplifies the implementation in both single and multi-robot scenarios. Conversely, while Arkin [ 86 ] acknowledged the benefits of such simplicity, his work delved into more intricate aspects of reactive control, including conflict resolution between behaviors and the inte- gration of reactive layers with higher-level planning when necessary. Ref. [ 87 ] examined that reactive agents respond instantly to stimuli based on predefined rules. Later, Ref. [ 88 ] extended the discussion to distributed systems, highlighting the nuances that arise when reactive agents are deployed in a decentralized, networked environment. Simple Reflex Agents [ 89 ], Behavior-Based Agents [ 90 ], Subsumption Archi- tecture Agents [ 91 ], Finite-State Machine (FSM) Reactive Agents [ 92 ], Hybrid Reactive Agents [ 93 ] are some examples of reactive agents. 3.2.2. Proactive agents Proactive agents anticipate future events and take the initiative to act before explicit instructions are given. These agents analyze patterns, predict needs, and make autonomous decisions to optimize outcomes [ 94 ]. By integrating predictive models, machine learning techniques, and advanced decision-making frameworks, proactive agents are poised to address challenges in fields ranging from au- tonomous vehicles and smart grids to healthcare and industrial au- tomation. Proactive agents can dynamically adjust their behavior based on feedback from the environment, leading to improved anticipatory performance over time [ 95 – 97 ]. Types of proactive AI agents, such as personal assistants [ 98 ] and predictive maintenance [ 99 , 100 ] tools, predict and address issues autonomously, optimize operations, and reduce costs in sectors like technology, healthcare, and manufactur- ing. Table 4 provides a comparison of reactive and proactive agent approaches, which outline their behaviors, advantages, and challenges. 3.2.3. Limited memory agents These agents retain historical data for a short duration, allowing them to improve decision making by analyzing past inputs [ 101 ]. sections.heading: External
sections.text: memory: Retrieval-augmented approaches accessing document stores, vector databases, or tool outputs. These hybrid approaches address limitations of pure parametric knowl- edge, including hallucination tendencies, knowledge cut-offs, and con- text window constraints. However, challenges remain in developing memory systems that efficiently balance comprehensiveness with re- trieval precision and integrate seamlessly with reasoning processes. Agentic AI systems rely heavily on high-fidelity memory to support tracking goals, plan over time, and engage in multistep conversa- tions. However, current memory types have key flaws. Parametric memory (inside the model) cannot be updated, leading to outdated knowledge. Working memory is limited in size, making it hard to handle long tasks. External memory systems, like databases, often return irrelevant or poorly ranked information. These gaps cause AI to forget, lose task focus, or make incorrect decisions. A better dynamic memory system is needed: one that can intelligently store, forget, and retrieve context based on the task at hand. Recent solutions aim to fix memory issues such as MemGPT [ 165 ] introduces a modular system that separates short-term, long-term, and episodic memory, helping agents recall key experiences across tasks. ReLoRA [ 166 ] and Streaming Transformers [ 167 ] enhance working memory by enabling longer context handling and reducing processing limits. Models like Retro [ 168 ], REALM [ 169 ], and KNN-LM [ 170 ] improve retrieval accuracy by using training signals to reduce irrelevant results. Latent cache distillation [ 171 ] integrates frequently retrieved knowledge back into the model’s internal memory for better grounding. A promising direction is agent-level memory policies [ 172 ], where AI learns what to store, when to retrieve it, and how to apply it in reasoning. These advances move toward smarter, more context-aware systems. However, it remains a challenge for researchers. Future agentic AI systems may incorporate centralized memory controllers that dynamically coordinate between parametric, working, and external memory, optimizing retrieval and storage based on task relevance and salience. Memory modules could become self-adaptive, learning to manage retention and forgetting through reinforcement learning, thereby enabling efficient memory use across diverse tasks. 3.3.3. Reasoning and decision-making Reasoning capabilities show perhaps the most dramatic progres- sion across our taxonomic framework, from simple condition-action mappings to sophisticated multistep reasoning processes. 79 U. Nisa, M. Shirazi, M.A. Saip et al. Journal of Automation and Intelligence 5 (2026) 69–89 • Reactive and Proactive Agents: Implement direct mappings from situations to actions, with limited or no explicit reasoning pro- cesses. Decision making is typically based on predefined rules or simple pattern matching. • Limited Memory and Model-Based Agents: Demonstrate basic inferential capabilities, including statistical reasoning and sim- ple causal modeling. These agents can evaluate alternative ac- tions through simulation, but typically rely on domain-specific heuristics. • Goal-Driven and Theory of Mind Agents: Exhibit more sophisti- cated planning and counterfactual reasoning, including multistep action sequences and consideration of others’ perspectives. These agents can decompose complex problems and adapt reasoning strategies to different domains. • Self-Aware Agents: Demonstrate metacognitive reasoning, includ- ing awareness of reasoning limitations, strategy selection, and self-correction. These agents can potentially engage in abstract reasoning across domains and generate novel problem solving approaches. sections.heading: Ensemble
sections.text: methods: Combining multiple reasoning approaches. Despite these advances, significant limitations remain in logical con- sistency, causal reasoning, and handling of complex, novel problem structures. Current systems still struggle with compositional general- ization and often exhibit reasoning failures when faced with problems requiring multiple interdependent inferences. These limitations arise when agentic systems focus on predicting the next word without ensur- ing logical consistency or understanding cause-and-effect. As a result, they struggle with complex tasks that require explicit symbolic rea- soning and causal structures. This leads to contradictory answers and missing dependencies, limiting their reliability in real-world applica- tions where long-term planning and consistent reasoning are essential. To address these challenges, researchers are developing methods like self-consistency decoding [ 173 ] to improve logical answers and neuro- symbolic integration to reduce contradictions using rule-based checks. Causal reasoning models such as CausalQA [ 174 , 175 ] and causal in- ference [ 176 ] help to distinguish true cause–effect relationships, while structured reasoning frameworks like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) [ 177 ] Tree-of-Thought [ 178 ], ReAct [ 69 ], and AutoGPT [ 179 ] enable better reflection and decision making in complex tasks. Researchers also use Neuro-Symbolic AI by combining large language models (LLMs) with symbolic reasoners such as theorem provers [ 180 ] and constraint solvers [ 181 ]. Moreover, giving agents access to external tools such as code interpreters and calculators enables them to handle complex calculations and verify their own reasoning steps. This shows that agentic AI systems are gradually moving toward building architectures that are structured for logical reasoning and decision-making. In the future, one possible solution can be to incor- porate training objectives into the optimization process that integrate logical consistency and formal verification. This would help agen- tic systems internally validate their reasoning rather than rely on sampling-based corrections. Agentic AI systems may use a combination of structured reasoning techniques, such as chain-of-thought prompting and self-reflection, to cross-verify their outputs, reduce logical errors, and enhance decision-making reliability. These approaches are key to building more reliable and adaptable agentic AI systems. 3.3.4. Learning and adaptation Learning mechanisms have evolved from the absence of adapta- tion in reactive agents to sophisticated multi-strategy approaches in advanced systems. • Reactive Agents lack learning capabilities, with behavior fixed at design time. • Proactive and Limited Memory Agents implement basic statistical learning and pattern recognition, enabling gradual adaptation to environmental regularities. • Model-Based and Goal-Driven Agents demonstrate more sophisti- cated learning through model updating, reinforcement learning, and transfer across related tasks. • Theory of Mind and Self-Aware Agents exhibit meta-learning capabilities, including learning how to learn, strategy adaptation, and curriculum self-generation. sections.heading: Continual
sections.text: learning: For accumulating capabilities without catastrophic forgetting. However, significant challenges remain in developing systems that can efficiently learn from limited data, transfer knowledge across dissimilar domains, and maintain performance across distribution shifts without extensive retraining. This is because the lack of lifelong learning and meta-learning capabilities makes agentic AI inefficient in dynamic and data-sparse conditions. This causes systems to struggle with limited supervision, unseen domains, or evolving tasks without retraining from scratch. To mitigate these problems, continual learning [ 182 ] en- abled agent architectures update memory modules, skill libraries, and planners incrementally using techniques such as experience replay, regularization, or generative pseudo-memory. Additionally, Meta-agent frameworks supporting fast adaptation, such as Meta-World [ 183 , 184 ] and LEAP [ 185 ]; domain-aware perception and planning modules that detect shifts and adjust internal behavior, like AgentAda [ 186 ]; and agent ecosystems that share knowledge between tasks or de- ployments, such as federated agent learning [ 187 ] and skill sharing protocols [ 188 ], are extensively explored. But meta-agent systems often fail to generalize to structurally different tasks and lack effective long- term memory consolidation for skill transfer. Domain-aware perception and planning are based on fixed adaptation rules and struggle in non-stationary or partially observable settings. Agent ecosystems face difficulties in synchronizing knowledge, managing diverse architec- tures, and ensuring privacy and consistency during communication, underscoring the need for more autonomous and adaptive agentic systems. In the future, exploration can focus on federated multi-agent re- inforcement learning and swarm learning, where agents learn from their local environments, share distilled skills periodically, and in- dependently validate incoming knowledge based on their own goals. This decentralized approach enables heterogeneous agents with varying sensors and roles to collaboratively update shared knowledge while maintaining autonomy and privacy, supporting scalable and adaptive agentic systems in dynamic, non-stationary environments. 80 U. Nisa, M. Shirazi, M.A. Saip et al. Journal of Automation and Intelligence 5 (2026) 69–89 3.3.5. Autonomy and initiative Autonomy levels vary substantially across agent types, from the rigid behavior of reactive systems to the self-directed operation of advanced agents. • Reactive and Proactive Agents demonstrate limited autonomy, operating within narrow predefined parameters with minimal initiative. • Limited Memory and Model-Based Agents exhibit increased op- erational autonomy, adapting to environmental variations and selecting from alternative approaches based on experience. • Goal-Driven and Theory of Mind Agents demonstrate strategic autonomy, independently determining sub-goals and action se- quences to achieve high-level objectives. • Self-Aware Agents potentially exhibit value autonomy, refining their own objectives and evaluation criteria through reflection and experience. The progression toward greater autonomy raises important questions about appropriate autonomy levels for different applications, control mechanisms, and value alignment. As noted by Ref. [ 189 ], ‘‘the prob- lem is not that machines might disobey us but that they might obey us too well’’ when objectives are misspecified or incomplete. This arises because agentic systems are often designed with predefined goals that lack alignment with human intent. When reward functions fail to capture ethical considerations, agents may overoptimize in unin- tended ways that violate social norms [ 190 ]. sections.text: intelligence: Recognizing and responding to human emotional states. However, challenges remain in developing systems that can navigate complex social dynamics, understand implicit communication, and adapt appropriately to diverse cultural contexts and individual pref- erences. These challenges stem from the fact that early agentic systems focused primarily on task execution rather than human interaction. They reacted to inputs without understanding people’s thoughts or emotions, and their responses were rigid, lacking personalization and cultural sensitivity. As a result, interactions felt robotic, limited, and socially unaware. As this area is still novel, researchers are actively exploring it by incorporating natural language interaction fluid human- agent collaboration [ 198 ] and personality modeling is used to ensure consistent behavior [ 199 ]. MetaMind [ 200 ] use Theory-of-Mind archi- tectures with specialized agents for mental state inference, cultural norms, and response generation, increasing social reasoning by 35.7%. Culturally adaptive systems such as CLCA [ 201 ] improve alignment through simulated role play to internalize implicit norms, while con- tinual personalization through reinforcement learning [ 202 ] tailors social behavior based on long-term feedback. Emerging architectural innovations propose ’Wisdom Layers’ meta-agent systems embedding reflective social cognition and causal ethics into agentic AI [ 203 ]. For agentic AI to function culturally intelligently, future systems must embrace adaptability, ethics, emotional awareness, and continual learning. For instance, use of layered agent designs such as Wisdom Layers combined with MetaMind’s separation of Theory-of-Mind rea- soning and action generation to improve coordination. In addition, integrate metacognitive modules that handle ethics, uncertainty, and long-term consequences. Additionally, researchers can explore virtual societies, meta-learning, and affective-causal reasoning to develop ad- vanced social strategies and emotionally aware behavior of agentic AI systems. 3.4. Environments of agentic AI The environments of agentic AI refer to the external or operational settings in which agentic AI systems operate. These examine the nature of the environment and their impact on AI behavior. Structurally, world environments are inherently complex and require agents to balance adaptability. For example, autonomous vehicles must navigate unpre- dictable traffic patterns [ 204 ], yet over adaptation risks instability in different scenarios. Table 7 presents a detailed overview of the various types of environment and their influence on AI behavior. Agentic AI is divided into two distinct phases: Physical agents [ 205 ] and virtual agents [ 206 ]. Physical environments, which are real-world autonomous systems like robots and self-driving cars, require real-time adaptabil- ity, safety, and interaction with dynamic, unstructured environments. While, virtual environments involve simulated tasks like game-playing AI or virtual assistants, offering scalable, controlled platforms for train- ing and testing. sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: This section examines the analysis, key challenges, and future di- rections in agentic AI research, focusing on evaluation difficulties, reliability issues, and problems inherited from the language models that power these agents. 4.1. Analysis Agentic AI is defined as autonomous systems capable of perceiving their environment, reasoning, and taking actions to achieve specific goals. These systems exhibit a level of agency akin to human decision- making, enabling them to operate independently without constant hu- man intervention. The operational framework of agentic AI integrates core intelligence, back-end decision making, and frontend interaction, allowing the system to continuously refine its operations through feed- back loops. This framework facilitates adaptive and intelligent decision making, distinguishing agentic AI from traditional AI systems that rely on explicit programming and human oversight. The evolution of agentic AI is marked by distinct phases, reflecting advancements in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and cogni- tive architectures. The early foundations (1980s–1990s) were rooted in symbolic reasoning and behavior-based AI, with a focus on inter- action with the environment rather than complex internal models. Key milestones during this period included the development of ra- tional agents, multiagent systems (MAS), and reinforcement learning (RL), which laid the groundwork for autonomous decision-making. The rise of learning-based agents (2001–2010) saw the integration of machine learning techniques, particularly neural networks, and re- inforcement learning, enabling more adaptive and scalable systems. This era also witnessed advancements in real-time object detection, multiagent reinforcement learning (MARL), and unsupervised learn- ing, which further enhanced the capabilities of agentic AI. The deep reinforcement learning era (2011–2017) marked a significant turning point, with the advent of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) enabling systems like deep Q-networks (DQN) to achieve human-level perfor- mance in complex tasks, such as playing video games and mastering strategic games like Go. This period also saw the emergence of self- improving agents capable of learning and adapting through self-play. The emergence of general-purpose agents (2018–2021) was character- ized by the introduction of large language models (LLMs) like GPT-3, which demonstrated the potential of general-purpose agents capable of reasoning and planning in diverse domains. This era marked a shift toward goal-directed capabilities and emergent cooperation among AI 82 U. Nisa, M. Shirazi, M.A. Saip et al. Journal of Automation and Intelligence 5 (2026) 69–89 agents. sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the evolution, key aspects, and challenges of agentic AI, which refers to autonomous AI systems capable of reasoning, decision-making, and adapting to dynamic environments. The evolution of agentic AI traces back to the 1980s, with foundational work in robotics and cognitive science, and has progressed through the rise of learning-based agents, the deep reinforcement learning era, and the emergence of general-purpose agents like GPT-3. Today, agentic AI is characterized by multi-modal and collaborative systems that integrate vision, language, and action for more autonomous and context-aware decision-making. The field has experienced a significant acceleration since 2018, with the emergence of large language model-based agents demonstrating capabilities that blur traditional boundaries between narrow and general AI systems. This acceleration shows no signs of slowing, with multi-modal and collaborative agent architectures representing the current frontier of development. Our taxonomic framework identifies a progressive spectrum of agent types, from reactive to self-aware systems, with each type building upon and extending the capabilities of previous generations. This tax- onomy provides a structured approach for understanding the diverse landscape of agentic systems and identifying capability gaps and de- velopment pathways. The paper identifies key patterns of agentic AI, such as tool use, reflection, planning, and multi-agent collaboration, and classifies agents into types like reactive, proactive, and self-aware agents, each suited for different tasks and environments. Agentic AI is driving transformation by enabling autonomous de- cision making, personalized services, and optimized resource man- agement. However, significant challenges remain, such as aligning AI goals with human values, ensuring adaptability in unpredictable environments, addressing resource constraints, and managing privacy and security risks. The paper also highlights the need for new regula- tory frameworks to address accountability and ethical concerns. Future research will focus on developing multi-modal and collaborative agents, improving scalability and efficiency, and advancing general-purpose agents capable of reasoning and self-improvement. Overall, agentic AI represents a significant leap toward autonomous, context-aware systems, but its safe and effective deployment will require address- ing technical, ethical, and regulatory challenges. The paper concludes that agentic AI is steadily moving from passive models to fully au- tonomous systems capable of reasoning, planning, and adapting in complex environments. As research continues to refine memory mech- anisms, alignment strategies, and multi-modal integration, agentic AI is expected to push further into domains requiring human-like creativ- ity, judgment, and autonomy. Although substantial progress has been made, important challenges remain in developing agentic systems that reason reliably, operate robustly across contexts, align with human values, and integrate effectively into existing sociotechnical systems. These challenges span technical, ethical, and governance dimensions, requiring interdisciplinary approaches to address effectively.
